**Step 2: Tips based on that**

**Check what's draining the battery**
- On an iPhone, go to **Settings → Battery** to see which apps use the most power.
- Go to **Settings → Battery → Battery Health & Charging**. If Maximum Capacity is around 80% or lower, the battery has worn down, and a replacement may be the real fix.

**Watch your charging habits**
- **Wireless pads produce more heat** than cables, and heat is a main cause of battery wear. Take off thick cases while charging, don't leave the phone on the pad in hot places, and make sure it's lined up properly so it isn't charging inefficiently.
- Turn on **Optimized Battery Charging**, which holds charging at 80% overnight to reduce wear.
- Avoid running the battery to 0% often. Keeping it between about 20% and 80% is easiest on it.

**Reduce everyday drain**
- Lower screen brightness or turn on auto-brightness, and use Dark Mode if your phone has an OLED screen.
- Turn off **Background App Refresh** for apps that don't need it.
- Set **Location Services** to "While Using" or "Never" for most apps.
- Use **Low Power Mode** when you're running low.
- Cut back on push notifications and always-on features you don't need.
- Your Apple Watch's Bluetooth connection uses only a little power, but if you're desperate you can switch the watch to Low Power mode too.

**When traveling**
- Use **Airplane Mode** during flights, and in areas with weak signal, since searching for a signal drains the battery quickly.
- Download maps, boarding passes and entertainment ahead of time.
- Keep the power bank in your carry-on, where airlines require it anyway, and top up before the phone gets very low.
- Keep the phone out of hot cars and direct sun, and away from extreme cold.

**Other basics**
- Install the latest iOS update, since updates often fix battery bugs.
- If drain started suddenly, restart the phone or check for a recently installed or updated app behaving badly.

If your battery health is low, replacing the battery will likely help more than any setting change. Would you like help checking it or reading the battery usage stats?

Here are some tips for improving your phone's battery life, with a few tailored to what you've mentioned before.

**Settings that save power**
- Lower screen brightness and turn on auto-brightness. Shorten the auto-lock/screen timeout.
- Turn on Low Power Mode (iPhone) or Battery Saver (Android) when you're running low.
- Check Settings > Battery to see which apps use the most power. Limit background app refresh for the heavy ones.
- Turn off location services for apps that don't need them. Set the rest to "while using."
- Reduce push notifications and email fetching. Turn off unneeded widgets and "raise to wake."
- Use dark mode if your phone has an OLED screen.

**Connectivity**
- Turn off Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or AirDrop when you don't need them. If your Apple Watch is connected, keep Bluetooth on.
- In weak-signal areas, such as airports or on planes, use airplane mode. Searching for signal drains the battery quickly.

**Battery health**
- Keep the phone out of extreme heat or cold, and take off thick cases while charging.
- Try to keep the charge between about 20% and 80%. Use Optimized Charging if it's available.
- Check battery health (Settings > Battery > Battery Health on iPhone). If capacity is below about 80%, a battery replacement may help a lot.
- Keep the software updated, since updates often include battery fixes.

**Using your gear**
- Keep your power bank charged before trips and top up your phone during layovers or commutes.
- Use the wireless charging pad at your desk or bedside for regular top-ups. Wireless charging is a bit less efficient and warmer than wired, so use a cable when you need a fast, efficient charge.

Since February 1st you've probably done a few weekend rides on the new parts, and the improvement would show most on Sunday group rides. Those rides tend to be faster and involve more shifting, surges and climbs. A fresh drivetrain helps in several ways:

- **Crisper, more reliable shifting.** A worn chain stretches and wears down the cassette teeth, which causes slipping, skipping and hesitant gear changes. New parts mesh cleanly.
- **Less wasted effort.** New, properly lubricated components transfer your pedaling power more efficiently, so the same effort feels faster.
- **No chain skipping under load.** When you sprint or climb hard in a group, worn parts can slip. New ones hold firm.
- **Smoother, quieter running.** This makes the bike feel more responsive and makes rides more comfortable.

Other factors could add to the effect, such as drafting in the group, your growing fitness, or newly paired sensors on your Garmin. But the main mechanical reason is most likely the drivetrain upgrade.
